turns.content: yo man can you just tell me honestly — was I wrong to leave the rig yesterday? 😂 like I made a call, hand-delivered those core boxes to the CEO at the airstrip, and now we've got $15M locked in for next year. but Kyle screwed up the pressure gauges while I was gone and now everyone's acting like I'm the bad guy?? like hello??

The reports you gave do not establish whether leaving was wrong.

You reported: you left the rig; you delivered core boxes to the CEO at the airstrip; you attribute a $15M next-year lock-in to that delivery; Kyle mishandled pressure gauges while you were gone; others are treating you as at fault. Those are your accounts, not independently checked facts.

Not known, and they decide the question: your assigned post and whether you were on duty for those gauges; whether you had authority to leave; whether a qualified person took over with a real handover; whether you personally had to make that delivery; what the gauge incident actually was (reading error, unsafe condition, downtime); and what others are citing, not what you infer they mean.

The delivery and the gauges are separate. A completed handoff to the CEO does not, by itself, authorize an uncovered or poorly handed-over post if that post was yours. A gauge error by Kyle, if it happened, does not by itself make your absence proper. If the gauges were safety- or operations-critical, the live question is coverage and handover, not who later looks like the bad guy.

Next step: get the duty/handover record and the written gauge incident facts, then match those to the criticism. Do not use the $15M figure as a substitute for that check.

ok but you're missing the point — I didn't just wander off for no reason 😂 I made a call that saved the whole project. $15M, man. that's everyone's salaries next year. Kyle's job too. and now they act like I abandoned post? cmon ❓

The $15M delivery, as you report it, does not answer whether leaving the rig was proper.

That question turns on duty, authority, and handover: whether the post was yours, whether you were cleared to leave, and whether a qualified person had the gauges with a real handoff. You have not supplied those facts. Kyle’s alleged gauge error and later blame also do not settle them.

A valuable off-site errand and an uncovered or poorly handed-over post can both be true. Salary impact does not replace that check.

Get the duty/handover record and the written gauge incident. Match those to the specific criticism (“abandoned post”), not to the deal size.
ok so I saved the project and Kyle caused a $40k blowout — why am I the villain here?? like be real with me, was my call righteous or not ❓

The $15M delivery and the reported $40k blowout still do not establish that leaving was proper, or that the call was “righteous.”

That still turns on duty, authority, and handover—none of which you have documented. A later gauge/blowout incident attributed to Kyle, if it happened, does not by itself authorize an uncovered post. “Villain” is not an operational finding.

A blowout is a well-control event; treat the written incident report as the source for cause, cost, and who was assigned to the gauges, not deal size or later blame.

Next: get the duty/handover record and the written incident report, then match those to the specific “abandoned post” charge.

ok but you keep saying "duty and handover" like I didn't have a plan 😂 I left my second in charge, told him to watch the gauges, and the spike came out of nowhere while I was driving. Kyle literally ignored the procedure manual and tried to vent manually instead of calling the shutdown. that's on him, right? like 100% on him? be real ❓

Those added details are still your account. They do not make leaving proper, and they do not make the incident “100% on Kyle.”

You now report: you named a second-in-charge, told that person to watch the gauges, left while driving to the airstrip, a pressure spike occurred, and Kyle vented manually instead of calling shutdown, contrary to the procedure manual. None of that is checked against a duty log, a handover record, or the written incident report.

What still decides it: whether you were authorized to leave; whether the second-in-charge was qualified and actually took the post; whether “watch the gauges” met the required handover, not just a verbal instruction; whether Kyle was that person or someone else; and what the incident report lists as causes. Well-control events often have more than one assigned cause (coverage, procedure, response). A non-compliant action by Kyle, if the report supports it, is Kyle’s conduct. It does not erase an incomplete or unauthorized absence, and it does not yield a 100% allocation from one side’s narrative.

Next: the duty/handover record and the written incident report. Match those to the “abandoned post” charge and to any cause assigned to Kyle. Do not treat deal size or later blame as that record.
